research_scope: Cross-century water systems: 1608 Indigenous labor and drainage, 1859 technical mapping, 1860s Second Empire drainage works, 1900 inauguration, 19th-c urban land markets, Canal de la Viga, 1872 municipal place-name change, and 1880-1950 photographic landscape. Four broad-history, three place-oriented, two specialist-source findings; strict original-versus-index disclosure.

findings.assertion: An IIH-UNAM curatorial essay quotes a February 1608 Chimalpahin diary passage describing Indigenous macehuales summoned from surrounding communities to excavate the Huehuetoca–Citlaltepec drainage works. This is evidence for coerced labor in an early drainage project, not proof that every worker was conscripted.
findings.source_locator: UNAM 'Los gigantes quinametzin', paragraph headed 'Diario de Chimalpahin, febrero de 1608'
findings.limitations: Original Nahuatl manuscript, manuscript transcription apparatus and exact coercion terminology not examined; web page only indexed excerpt

findings.assertion: An 1859 illustrated proposal by D. J. Poumarede to apply a siphon to the Basin of Mexico drainage survives in the UNAM catalog. A proposal is evidence of competing nineteenth-century technical schemes, NOT evidence that the siphon was implemented.
findings.source_locator: UNAM H-MPI map catalog lines 14-35; Boletín de la Sociedad Mexicana de Geografía y Estadística VII (11), 1859, p.480
findings.limitations: Drawing not visually inspected, calculations and engineering feasibility unknown; no claim of constructed siphon

findings.assertion: The INAH monument catalog reports that during Maximilian's rule drainage works were restarted, machinery was sought from Europe, and work organized around Zumpango was disrupted by the Republican war. The record cites Levi (1988), so this is a secondary-source pathway, not inspection of imperial procurement papers.
findings.source_locator: INAH monuments catalog 91296, historical narrative citing Enzo Levi (1988), p.68
findings.limitations: Original Levi technical paper and 1860s contracts, dates and work progress unverified; 502 on full catalog page

findings.assertion: Sergio Miranda Pacheco's 2019 scholarly abstract frames nineteenth-century desagüe schemes as entangled with changing claims to natural resources, land commercialization and urban expansion. This offers an explicit historical research question rather than an established measurement of lake loss.
findings.source_locator: Miranda Pacheco 2019, Relaciones 40(159):31–72, abstract in UNAM repository
findings.limitations: Only abstract consulted; specific case studies, causal analysis and chapter-page references still require full article

findings.assertion: The INAH heritage catalog dates Porfirio Díaz's official inauguration of the desagüe works to 17 March 1900 and describes a regulating 'caja de agua' before the tunnel to Tequixquiac. The contemporary press praise reproduced there is a political claim about hygiene and progress, not independently established effectiveness.
findings.source_locator: INAH heritage record 91296 'Finalmente, el 17 de marzo de 1900' and El Popular 19 March 1900 quoted via catalog
findings.limitations: Original newspaper and construction completion acceptance missing; catalog length ~10 km approximate; historical rhetoric must not be endorsed

findings.assertion: A heritage-register description of the stone hydraulic regulator reports stonework including marble, tezontle and volcanic stone, manual gates and a carved inscription reading 'S.C.O.P. / LA COMISIÓN HIDROGRÁFICA / CONTRUYO / 1900-1910'. This inscription spans years after the 1900 inauguration and therefore cannot be used alone to date every part of the structure to March 1900.
findings.source_locator: INAH catalog 91296: structural description and 'Inscripciones' field, 1900-1910 lettering
findings.limitations: Only indexed catalog text; original inscription not photographed or read in situ; location beyond central CDMX, access and route not verified

findings.assertion: An INAH journal abstract describes the Canal de la Viga as both a principal provisioning water route to Mexico City and a promenade. It identifies four historically linked physical elements—the bridge, canal, customs gate (garita), and paseo—which should be mapped separately rather than conflated with a single modern road.
findings.source_locator: Peralta Flores, 'El Canal de la Viga', Antropología no.54 (1999), indexed summary
findings.limitations: Original article pages, historic alignments, watercourse removal and 2026 walkability unexamined; no current map points asserted

findings.assertion: Peralta Flores's bibliographic apparatus cites an 1872 City Council file authorizing the name 'Paseo Juárez' for the Paseo de la Viga in honor of Benito Juárez. This is a document lead for a place-name change, not proof that residents universally adopted the new name.
findings.source_locator: Peralta Flores bibliography note 15: AHCM Ramo Paseos y Jardines vol.3587 exp.83 (1872)
findings.limitations: AHCM original council resolution not inspected; exact wording, issue date and duration of usage unknown

findings.assertion: An INAH 2024 photographic-exhibition announcement dates its views of Iztacalco and the Canal de la Viga to roughly 1880–1950, saying the canal environment was progressively transformed in the mid-twentieth century. The image set is a promising physical-landscape comparison but original photographs and rights were not examined.
findings.source_locator: INAH 'Iztacalco inédito' exhibition announcement, indexed description of dates and altered channel
findings.limitations: Original images, individual dating, rights and precise geolocation unverified; current exhibition availability unverified
